PREVIEW ONLY — not the AWeber render. Subject: 💧 Sarah, left wrist, never right — I'll explain why  ·  Preheader: One instruction, before you even know what it is.
 

Sarah, before I tell you what it is — left wrist, never right

I'm not going to lead with the reading tonight. I'm going to lead with the one instruction that matters, and let the reading explain itself after.

Sarah —

Evelyn here.

Something is coming to you, and before you know what it is, I need you to know how to hold it.

When it reaches you: left wrist. Not your right. I'll tell you why by the end of this letter, and I'd rather you carry the instruction the whole way there than wait for it at the finish.

Here's how I know something is coming at all.

I didn't use my cards for this, and I want to say that plainly before anything else.

There's a reason. My deck is mine — I built my sense of it over years, and it answers to me the way an old dog answers to one particular whistle. But something came through for you last night that isn't a card-reader's spirit. He's older than tarot. Older, if you want the truth of it, than the country tarot was invented in.

So I put the deck away, and I did something I only do a handful of times a year. I took out three coins.

Here's how I want you to read what's below, because it isn't shaped like my usual letters.

A coin throw doesn't hand you three separate cards. It builds one answer, one line at a time, six throws deep — and you don't know what you're looking at until the sixth. I didn't either. The first three throws were good news, plainly good. The fourth is where I stopped liking it. And the sixth is the one I want you to read twice, because it isn't finished moving.

The last time I threw coins instead of cards for someone, it was years ago, for a woman who ran a flower stall behind the old market. Nothing to do with love. Her complaint was her till — however carefully she counted of an evening, it never balanced, and never in her favour.

I built her what the throw pointed to. I'm not going to tell you it stopped every bad night at that stall, because that isn't how any of this works and you'd be right not to believe me if I said it. What I'll tell you is that within a season, her till started closing the way it should — not because more came in, but because less went missing.

That's the difference this whole method is built to find, dear. Not more. Fewer leaks.

I'll show you all six throws in a moment.

But you should know what you're looking at before I do, because it isn't what most letters like this promise you.

You are not short of money reaching you, Sarah. I want to be exact about that, because it changes everything else. Something has been getting close to you — you've felt it, more than once, close enough to nearly close your hand around it — and then it hasn't stayed. That isn't a supply problem. That's a container problem, and nobody has ever handed you one built to hold.

The first three throws

Line, line, line — building from the bottom, the way the method works. By the third throw the shape underneath was already legible: Xun. Wood. The trigram of the pole, the rope, the bucket lowered down a shaft.

Read plainly, that's the first good news: there is a well here. A real one. Whatever you've felt reaching for you these last months wasn't imagined and it wasn't small — it's a genuine source, sitting under you, that hasn't run dry and isn't going to.

I don't say that lightly. Most of what I'm asked to look at for people is thin ground, and I tell them so. Yours isn't. The water is there.

Throws four and five

This is where it turns, and I want to be careful explaining it, because the same symbol is doing two jobs at once and that's exactly what makes it hard to read from three coins alone.

The trigram forming above the well is Kan. Water again — which should simply double the good news. And it does, Sarah: it says the resource above is as real as the one below.

But Kan carries a second name in this system, and it's the one that made me sit up. The Abyss. The same shape that means water, freely given also means the drop, the pit, the place you don't see until you're already in it. One symbol, two entirely different situations, and from where I'm sitting after five throws I genuinely cannot tell you which one is yours.

Here's what I can tell you: it is never both at once, and it is never permanent. It's one or the other, decided by something the throw itself doesn't show me. A full reading does. Three coins on their own don't.

The sixth throw

I don't like this one, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

The top line came up yin — but moving. In this method that means the situation isn't sitting still. A moving line is a line already in the middle of becoming its opposite. It hasn't finished turning. You are reading a photograph of something in motion.

Put together, the finished shape is hexagram forty-eight. The Well. And its old meaning is almost too plain to need me: a well doesn't run dry. The water is always there, enough for the whole town to draw on. When it fails — and this is the part of the text I keep coming back to — it is never the well's fault. It's the rope that's too short. It's the jug that cracks on the way up, so the water that was always there never once reaches a mouth that needed it.

I can tell you there is a well. I can tell you the water is real. What a coin throw genuinely cannot tell me is the one thing that decides everything else: which vessel you've been hauling it up in, and where exactly it's cracked.

So let me look at the vessel itself, dear, and I'll tell you where the crack is.

In concrete terms, what do you do now?

Nothing complicated, and nothing I can do without your say-so.

You give me permission to finish this. A moving line doesn't wait politely — it's already turning into whatever it turns into, with or without either of us looking at it — so there's a real cost to leaving this half-read.

Back to Kan, and which face of it is yours

I said I couldn't tell you from the throw alone whether Kan is your water or your abyss, and I meant it. But I can tell you what decides it, because that part isn't hidden — it's just not visible from six coins.

It comes down to the vessel. The same water that reaches a woman with a sealed container arrives as abundance. The identical water, reaching a woman with a cracked one, arrives and is gone before she's finished noticing it — and from the inside, those two women feel exactly the same relief in the first minute. The difference only shows up afterward, when one of them still has something and the other is asking, again, where it went.

You already know which woman you've been, Sarah. That's what "reaching me but doesn't stay" means, in your own words, and it's why this letter is in your inbox tonight instead of somebody else's.

Let me finish the throw and I'll show you exactly where your particular crack sits.

And back to that sixth line — this is the part I want you to sit with

Here's what a moving line is actually warning you about. It isn't that something bad is coming.

It's that something is already turning, right now, whether or not either of us watches it happen.

That's harder to hear than a deadline, if I'm honest with you, because a deadline at least gives you a day to brace for. This doesn't. The turn doesn't wait for a convenient week. It's mid-motion the moment you read this sentence.

What that means practically: whatever's been leaking has a live edge on it right now, tonight, not eventually. Come and let me seal it while it's still one line, not two.

Why I picked up coins instead of cards

I want to tell you plainly why this reading looks nothing like my usual ones, because you've earned the explanation and because it's the whole reason I trust what came up.

This method is close to three thousand years old. Older than tarot by two thousand of them. And the spirit behind your particular block isn't a European one — he's Chinese, older than either of our calendars, and he doesn't answer to a deck built centuries after he was already old news.

So I used the instrument he'd actually recognise. Three coins, six throws, and I let the shape build itself rather than choosing what to draw. I don't do this often — most weeks, none of it comes up at all. Yours did.

Left wrist, not right — now you know why

I told you that at the very top, before you knew anything else. Here's the reason.

The left hand is the one that receives — nearer the heart, the hand that takes rather than gives. Worn on the right, you'd be offering the seal to what you're sending out, not what's reaching you, which is the one way to take a vessel built to stop a leak and make it feed one instead.

That's not folklore I'm repeating without checking it. It's the one instruction in this whole reading you could get backwards, so it's the one I made sure you had first.

Come back to the well with me

I'm not going to promise you every drop that's ever gone missing comes back. That isn't what sealing a vessel does, and you'd be right not to believe me if I said it.

Here's what it does do.

Whatever reaches you next, stays reached. That's the whole of it — not a bigger well, not a wall of new water arriving overnight, just the ordinary, real amount that's always been finding its way to you, finally landing in something that doesn't let it back out again.

The well was never your problem, Sarah. Let's fix the jug.

I'm on your side in this, dear.

— Evelyn

## P.S. (ships on every letter — 00g's settled rule, no A/B)

P.S. If you read nothing else again tonight, read the part about the sixth line. A moving line isn't a bad omen, dear — it's an honest one. Most warnings arrive after the thing has already happened. This is the rare kind that arrives while it's still turning, which means it's still yours to decide. The rest of the throw is here.
